title: Ha'azinu: ask your father (Deuteronomy 32:7)
hookLine: remember the days of old; ask your father and your elders
tomorrow: Ha'azinu: the eagle over its nest (Deuteronomy 32:11)

cards: A woman sits at her grandmother's funeral, and the questions start to arrive. Not about what was said. About what was never asked.
How did you two meet? What was your own grandfather like? What was the hardest year of your life?
The answers went with her. In the middle of Ha'azinu, between the Rock and the history of the people, Moses' song gives an instruction aimed at exactly that loss.

teach.b: "Remember the days of old, Consider the years of many generations; Ask thy father, and he will declare unto thee, Thine elders, and they will tell thee." Two pairs. Remember and consider: work you do inside your own head.
Ask and be told: work that needs another person. The verse doesn't trust memory alone. You have to go and ask.
Father and elders form a kind of ladder. Your father knows his own years. The elders reach further back.
And Jewish tradition is built like that ladder.

teach.h: MOSES TO JOSHUA TO THE ELDERS.
teach.b: The tractate Pirkei Avot opens with a chain: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly.
Each link asked, and was told. The Passover seder runs on asking too. The night is shaped around a child's questions.
Notice where the verse puts the responsibility.
On the younger one. Ask. The elders' part is to declare and to tell, but they can only answer what someone thinks to ask.

Some old people carry stories no one has ever asked for. Some families have one person who knows where everyone came from, and limited time to tell it. The song puts it plainly: memory isn't only kept.
It has to be asked for.

how: Jewish learning is built on chains of transmission, from teacher to student and parent to child; Pirkei Avot opens with that chain, and the Passover seder is structured around children's questions.

o: give ear: the song's first word, to the sky
be silent: the song's call for quiet
these words: the name of Deuteronomy

games.q: inside the song's instruction — tap the pairs.
p: and he will declare unto thee

s: the verse says memory alone is enough
it adds: ask, and be told.
Pirkei Avot opens with a chain of teachers beginning with Moses
Moses to Joshua, to the elders, to the prophets.
in the verse, the elders are told to go and teach the young
the younger one is told to ask.

games.q: you want to know where your family came from. after remembering and considering, what does the verse tell you to do?
o: wait for someone to tell you.
ask your father and your elders.
games.why: 'ask thy father, and he will declare unto thee': the asking falls to the younger one.

practice: Think of the oldest person you could reach, a parent, a grandparent, an old neighbor, someone at your congregation, and what you don't know about their life.
Choose one question, not a quiz but a door: who taught you to cook, or what do you remember about your own grandparents?

wordCard.voice: Ha'azinu. Give ear. And in it, a command to ask: ask thy father, thine elders.

carryVoice: Your line: ask your elders. They can only answer what someone thinks to ask. That's day five hundred thirty.
